claim: Neurons in higher cortical areas, such as the prefrontal cortex, are often tuned to a variety of sensory and motor variables.
source: Neurons in higher cortical areas, such as the prefrontal cortex, are often tuned to a variety of sensory and motor variables, and are therefore said to display mixed selectivity.
evidence: This is a statement about neural properties in prefrontal cortex, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Neurons in higher cortical areas display mixed selectivity.
source: Neurons in higher cortical areas, such as the prefrontal cortex, are often tuned to a variety of sensory and motor variables, and are therefore said to display mixed selectivity.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established neuroscience terminology.

claim: The complexity of single neuron responses can obscure what information higher cortical areas represent and how it is represented.
source: This complexity of single neuron responses can obscure what information these areas represent and how it is represented.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based claim about the interpretational challenges posed by mixed selectivity.

claim: Demixed principal component analysis (dPCA) decomposes population activity into a few components.
source: Here we demonstrate the advantages of a new dimensionality reduction technique, demixed principal component analysis (dPCA), that decomposes population activity into a few components.
evidence: This is a description of the method presented in the manuscript.

claim: dPCA systematically captures the majority of the variance of the data.
source: In addition to systematically capturing the majority of the variance of the data, dPCA also exposes the dependence of the neural representation on task parameters such as stimuli, decisions, or rewards.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results shown in Figures 3-6c throughout the manuscript.

claim: dPCA exposes the dependence of neural representation on task parameters such as stimuli, decisions, or rewards.
source: In addition to systematically capturing the majority of the variance of the data, dPCA also exposes the dependence of the neural representation on task parameters such as stimuli, decisions, or rewards.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the demixed components shown in Figures 3-6b.

claim: The authors reanalyzed population data from four datasets comprising different species, different cortical areas and different experimental tasks.
source: To illustrate our method we reanalyze population data from four datasets comprising different species, different cortical areas and different experimental tasks.
evidence: The manuscript presents analyses of four different datasets as shown in Figures 3-6.

claim: dPCA provides a concise way of visualizing data that summarizes task-dependent features of population response in a single figure.
source: In each case, dPCA provides a concise way of visualizing the data that summarizes the task-dependent features of the population response in a single figure.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3-6 where each dataset is summarized in a single comprehensive figure.

claim: Neural responses in higher-order areas display baffling heterogeneity even when animals carry out simple tasks.
source: This problem has been particularly severe in higher-order areas such as the prefrontal cortex, where neural responses display a baffling heterogeneity, even if animals are carrying out rather simple tasks (Brody et al., 2003; Machens et al., 2010; Hernández et al., 2010; Mante et al., 2013; Rigotti et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In neurophysiological studies, it is common practice to pre-select cells based on particular criteria and then average their firing rates.
source: In neurophysiological studies, it is common practice to pre-select cells based on particular criteria, such as responsiveness to the same stimulus, and to then average the firing rates of the pre-selected cells.
evidence: This describes a standard methodological approach in the field.

claim: Pre-selecting and averaging cells eliminates much of the richness of single-cell activities.
source: This practice eliminates much of the richness of single-cell activities, similar to imaging techniques with low spatial resolution, such as MEG, EEG, or fMRI.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of traditional methods based on reasoning about information loss.

claim: Population averages ignore much of the fine structure of single cell responses.
source: While population averages can identify some of the information that higher-order areas process, they ignore much of the fine structure of the single cell responses (Wohrer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Most neurons in higher cortical areas typically encode several task parameters simultaneously.
source: Indeed, most neurons in higher cortical areas will typically encode several task parameters simultaneously, and therefore display what has been termed mixed selectivity (Rigotti et al., 2013; Pagan and Rust, 2014; Park et al., 2014; Raposo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Several dimensionality reduction methods have been developed specifically for electrophysiological data in recent years.
source: In recent years, several such methods have been developed that are specifically targeted to electrophysiological data, working on the level of single spikes (Pfau et al., 2013), accommodating different time scales of latent variables (Yu et al., 2009), or accounting for the dynamics of the population response (Buesing et al., 2012a; 2012b; Churchland et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior methodological work.

claim: Existing dimensionality reduction approaches reduce dimensionality without taking task parameters into account.
source: However, these approaches reduce the dimensionality of the data without taking task parameters, i.e., sensory and motor variables controlled or monitored by the experimenter, into account.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of existing methods based on their design.

claim: Mixed selectivity remains in the data even after dimensionality reduction with existing methods.
source: Consequently, mixed selectivity remains in the data even after the dimensionality reduction step.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of methods not accounting for task parameters.

claim: The problem of mixed selectivity can be addressed by dimensionality reduction methods that are informed by task parameters.
source: The problem can be addressed by dimensionality reduction methods that are informed by the task parameters (Machens et al., 2010; Machens, 2010; Brendel et al., 2011; Mante et al., 2013; Raposo et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work including the authors' own previous work.

claim: The authors previously introduced a dimensionality reduction technique called demixed principal component analysis (dPCA).
source: We have previously introduced a dimensionality reduction technique, demixed principal component analysis (dPCA) (Brendel et al., 2011), that emphasizes two goals.
evidence: This is a statement about the authors' prior work with citation.

claim: The previous version of dPCA aimed to find a decomposition of data into latent components that are easily interpretable with respect to task parameters.
source: It aims to find a decomposition of the data into latent components that (a) are easily interpretable with respect to the experimentally controlled and monitored task parameters; and (b) preserve the original data as much as possible, ensuring that no valuable information is thrown away.
evidence: This describes the design goals of the method.

claim: The previous version of dPCA aimed to preserve the original data as much as possible.
source: It aims to find a decomposition of the data into latent components that (a) are easily interpretable with respect to the experimentally controlled and monitored task parameters; and (b) preserve the original data as much as possible, ensuring that no valuable information is thrown away.
evidence: This describes the design goals of the method.

claim: The new version of dPCA has the same objectives as the older version.
source: The new version of the method has the same objectives as the older version (Brendel et al., 2011), but is more principled, more flexible, and has an analytical solution, meaning that it does not suffer from any numerical optimization problems.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current and previous versions of the method.

claim: The new version of dPCA is more principled than the older version.
source: The new version of the method has the same objectives as the older version (Brendel et al., 2011), but is more principled, more flexible, and has an analytical solution, meaning that it does not suffer from any numerical optimization problems.
evidence: This is a comparative claim about methodological improvements.

claim: The new version of dPCA is more flexible than the older version.
source: The new version of the method has the same objectives as the older version (Brendel et al., 2011), but is more principled, more flexible, and has an analytical solution, meaning that it does not suffer from any numerical optimization problems.
evidence: This is a comparative claim about methodological improvements.

claim: The new version of dPCA has an analytical solution.
source: The new version of the method has the same objectives as the older version (Brendel et al., 2011), but is more principled, more flexible, and has an analytical solution, meaning that it does not suffer from any numerical optimization problems.
evidence: This is a technical claim about the mathematical properties of the method.

claim: The new version of dPCA does not suffer from numerical optimization problems.
source: The new version of the method has the same objectives as the older version (Brendel et al., 2011), but is more principled, more flexible, and has an analytical solution, meaning that it does not suffer from any numerical optimization problems.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of having an analytical solution.

claim: The new mathematical formulation highlights similarities to and differences from PCA and LDA.
source: Furthermore, the new mathematical formulation highlights similarities to and differences from related well-known methods such as principal component analysis (PCA) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 and the Materials and methods section.

claim: The dPCA code is available at http://github.com/machenslab/dPCA for Matlab and Python.
source: The dPCA code is available at http://github.com/machenslab/dPCA for Matlab and Python.
evidence: This is a factual statement about code availability.

claim: Monkeys in the somatosensory working memory task were required to discriminate two vibratory stimuli presented to the fingertip.
source: In this task, monkeys were required to discriminate two vibratory stimuli presented to the fingertip.
evidence: This describes the experimental paradigm with citations to the original studies.

claim: The stimuli F1 and F2 in the somatosensory task were separated by a 3 s delay.
source: The stimuli F1 and F2 were separated by a 3 s delay, and the monkeys had to report which stimulus had a higher frequency by pressing one of the two available buttons (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental paradigm shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Monkeys had to report which stimulus had a higher frequency by pressing one of two available buttons.
source: The stimuli F1 and F2 were separated by a 3 s delay, and the monkeys had to report which stimulus had a higher frequency by pressing one of the two available buttons (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental paradigm shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The PSTHs of many neurons are tuned to the stimulus F1, the decision, or both.
source: We find that the PSTHs of many neurons are tuned to the stimulus F1, the decision, or both (Figure 1b; so-called mixed selectivity), and different neurons generally show different tuning.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Different neurons generally show different tuning in the somatosensory task.
source: We find that the PSTHs of many neurons are tuned to the stimulus F1, the decision, or both (Figure 1b; so-called mixed selectivity), and different neurons generally show different tuning.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The two components from the ANOVA-based approach explain only 23% of the total variance of the population firing rates.
source: Indeed, the two components from Figure 1e explain only 23% of the total variance of the population firing rates and the two components from Figure 1h explain only 22% (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The two components from the TDR approach explain only 22% of the total variance.
source: Indeed, the two components from Figure 1e explain only 23% of the total variance of the population firing rates and the two components from Figure 1h explain only 22% (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis shown in Figure 1h.

claim: The first six principal components explain 69% of variance in the somatosensory task data.
source: However, the weights to form these linear combinations are chosen so as to maximize the amount of explained variance (first six components explain 69% of variance, see Figure 1i–k).
evidence: This is a quantitative result shown in Figure 1i.

claim: PCA paints a more complex picture of population activity than supervised methods, dominated by strong temporal dynamics.
source: Indeed, PCA paints a much more complex picture of the population activity, dominated by strong temporal dynamics, with several stimulus- and decision-related components.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing Figure 1k with Figures 1e and 1h.

claim: Even supervised methods show decision-related activity in stimulus components and stimulus-related activity in decision components.
source: At the same time, none of the methods can fully demix the stimulus and decision information: even the supervised methods show decision-related activity in the stimulus components and stimulus-related activity in the decision components (Figure 1e,h).
evidence: This observation is visible in Figures 1e and 1h.

claim: The goals of demixing and compression generally constitute a trade-off.
source: We will first explain that these two goals generally constitute a trade-off, then suggest a solution to this trade-off for a single task parameter, and then generalize to multiple task parameters.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the toy example in Figure 2.

claim: LDA projection separates stimuli better than dPCA projection but does not preserve information about distance between classes.
source: Figure 2b,f,h provides a toy example of a situation when these two goals yield very different solutions: the LDA projection separates the three classes better than the dPCA projection, but the dPCA projection preserves the information about the distance between classes.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the toy example shown in Figure 2.

claim: The reduced-rank regression problem can be solved via singular value decomposition.
source: This problem is known as reduced-rank regression (RRR) (Izenman, 1975; Reinsel and Velu, 1998; Izenman, 2008) and can be solved via the singular value decomposition.
evidence: This is a mathematical fact about reduced-rank regression with citations.

claim: The dataset analyzed from the somatosensory working memory task encompasses 832 neurons from two animals.
source: We first applied dPCA to the dataset presented above (Romo et al., 1999; Brody et al., 2003), encompassing 832 neurons from two animals.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the dataset with citations.

claim: Each neuron in the PFC dataset has a distinct response pattern.
source: As is typical for PFC, each neuron has a distinct response pattern and many neurons show mixed selectivity (some examples are shown in Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the examples shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Many neurons in the PFC dataset show mixed selectivity.
source: As is typical for PFC, each neuron has a distinct response pattern and many neurons show mixed selectivity (some examples are shown in Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the examples shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The overall variance explained by dPCA components is very close to the overall variance explained by PCA components.
source: The overall variance explained by the dPCA components (Figure 3c, red line) is very close to the overall variance explained by the PCA components (black line).
evidence: This is shown quantitatively in Figure 3c.

claim: Barely any variance was lost by imposing the demixing constraint in dPCA.
source: Accordingly, we barely lost any variance by imposing the demixing constraint, and the population activity is accurately represented by the obtained dPCA components.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison shown in Figure 3c.

claim: dPCA captures the persistence of F1 tuning during the delay period.
source: The dPCA analysis captures the major findings previously obtained with these data: the persistence of the F1 tuning during the delay period (component #5; Romo et al., 1999; Machens et al., 2005), the temporal dynamics of short-term memory (components ##5, 10, 13; Brody et al., 2003; Machens et al., 2010; Barak et al., 2010), the 'ramping' or 'climbing' activities in the delay period (components ##1–3; Brody et al., 2003; Machens et al., 2010); and pronounced decision-related activities (component #6, Jun et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by component #5 in Figure 3b and citations to prior work.

claim: dPCA captures the temporal dynamics of short-term memory.
source: The dPCA analysis captures the major findings previously obtained with these data: the persistence of the F1 tuning during the delay period (component #5; Romo et al., 1999; Machens et al., 2005), the temporal dynamics of short-term memory (components ##5, 10, 13; Brody et al., 2003; Machens et al., 2010; Barak et al., 2010), the 'ramping' or 'climbing' activities in the delay period (components ##1–3; Brody et al., 2003; Machens et al., 2010); and pronounced decision-related activities (component #6, Jun et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by components #5, 10, 13 in Figure 3b and citations to prior work.

claim: dPCA captures 'ramping' or 'climbing' activities in the delay period.
source: The dPCA analysis captures the major findings previously obtained with these data: the persistence of the F1 tuning during the delay period (component #5; Romo et al., 1999; Machens et al., 2005), the temporal dynamics of short-term memory (components ##5, 10, 13; Brody et al., 2003; Machens et al., 2010; Barak et al., 2010), the 'ramping' or 'climbing' activities in the delay period (components ##1–3; Brody et al., 2003; Machens et al., 2010); and pronounced decision-related activities (component #6, Jun et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by components #1-3 in Figure 3b and citations to prior work.

claim: dPCA captures pronounced decision-related activities.
source: The dPCA analysis captures the major findings previously obtained with these data: the persistence of the F1 tuning during the delay period (component #5; Romo et al., 1999; Machens et al., 2005), the temporal dynamics of short-term memory (components ##5, 10, 13; Brody et al., 2003; Machens et al., 2010; Barak et al., 2010), the 'ramping' or 'climbing' activities in the delay period (components ##1–3; Brody et al., 2003; Machens et al., 2010); and pronounced decision-related activities (component #6, Jun et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by component #6 in Figure 3b and citation to prior work.

claim: The decision components resemble derivatives of each other.
source: We note that the decision components resemble derivatives of each other; these higher-order derivatives likely arise due to slight variations in the timing of responses across neurons (see Appendix B for more details).
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3b with a theoretical explanation in Appendix B.

claim: Higher-order derivatives in decision components likely arise due to slight variations in timing of responses across neurons.
source: We note that the decision components resemble derivatives of each other; these higher-order derivatives likely arise due to slight variations in the timing of responses across neurons (see Appendix B for more details).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation provided in Appendix B.

claim: Stimulus representation rotates in neural space during the delay period.
source: In particular, plotting the first two stimulus components against each other (see Video 1) illustrates how stimulus representation rotates in the neural space during the delay period so that the encoding subspaces during F1 and F2 periods are not the same (but far from orthogonal either).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Video 1.

claim: The encoding subspaces during F1 and F2 periods are not the same but far from orthogonal.
source: In particular, plotting the first two stimulus components against each other (see Video 1) illustrates how stimulus representation rotates in the neural space during the delay period so that the encoding subspaces during F1 and F2 periods are not the same (but far from orthogonal either).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Video 1.

claim: The visuospatial working memory dataset contains 956 neurons recorded in the lateral PFC of two monkeys.
source: We analyzed the activity of 956 neurons recorded in the lateral PFC of two monkeys performing this task.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the dataset.

claim: Stimulus and decision are well separated at the population level in the visuospatial task despite being intermingled at the single-neuron level.
source: As before, stimulus and decision are well separated at the population level despite being intermingled at the single-neuron level; at the same time dPCA captures almost the same amount of variance as PCA.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4b.

claim: dPCA captures almost the same amount of variance as PCA in the visuospatial task.
source: As before, stimulus and decision are well separated at the population level despite being intermingled at the single-neuron level; at the same time dPCA captures almost the same amount of variance as PCA.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Task-specific components appear in population activity only after extensive training.
source: These task-specific components appear in the population activity only after extensive training.
evidence: This is based on comparison of pre-training and post-training data, consistent with prior findings.

claim: The olfactory discrimination dataset contains 437 neurons recorded in five rats.
source: We analyzed the activity of 437 neurons recorded in five rats in four conditions: two stimuli (left and right) each paired with two decisions (left and right).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the dataset.

claim: Neurons in rat OFC exhibit diverse firing patterns and mixed selectivity.
source: Just as neurons from monkey PFC, neurons in rat OFC exhibit diverse firing patterns and mixed selectivity (Feierstein et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Interaction components in the olfactory discrimination task separate rewarded and unrewarded conditions.
source: In this dataset, interaction components separate rewarded and unrewarded conditions (thick and thin lines in Figure 5b, bottom row), i.e., correspond to neurons tuned either to reward, or to the absence of reward.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Interaction components are by far the most prominent among all condition-dependent components in the olfactory discrimination task.
source: Interaction components are by far the most prominent among all the condition-dependent components, corresponding to the observation that many neurons are tuned to the presence/absence of reward.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5d and consistent with prior findings.

claim: Stimulus components show clear stimulus tuning even in error trials in the olfactory discrimination task.
source: Stimulus components are less prominent, but nevertheless show clear stimulus tuning, demonstrating that even in error trials there is reliable information about stimulus identity in the population activity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Neurons tuned to presence/absence of reward start firing before reward delivery in the olfactory discrimination task.
source: Curiously, the first interaction component (#4) already shows significant tuning to reward in the anticipation period. In other words, neurons tuned to presence/absence of reward start firing before the reward delivery (or, on error trials, before the reward could have been delivered).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b, component #4.

claim: The olfactory categorization dataset contains 214 OFC neurons from three rats.
source: We analyzed the activity of 214 OFC neurons from three rats recorded in 8 conditions, corresponding to four odor mixtures, each paired with two decisions (left and right).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the dataset.

claim: The second interaction component in the olfactory categorization task can be interpreted as corresponding to the rat's uncertainty or confidence about its own choice.
source: The characteristic U-shape for the error trials and the inverted U-shape for the correct trials agrees well with the predicted value of the rat's uncertainty in each condition (Kepecs et al., 2008). Accordingly, this component can be interpreted as corresponding to the rat's uncertainty or confidence about its own choice, confirming the results of Kepecs et al. (2008).
evidence: This interpretation is based on the pattern shown in Figure 6b inset and agreement with prior work.

claim: Most of the variance of neural activity is captured by condition-independent components that amount to 65-90% of signal variance.
source: First, most of the variance of the neural activity is always captured by the condition-independent components that together amount to 65–90% of the signal variance (see pie charts in Figures 3–6d; see Materials and methods for definition of 'signal variance').
evidence: This is shown quantitatively in the pie charts in Figures 3-6d.

claim: Condition-independent components capture temporal modulations of neural activity throughout the trial, irrespective of task condition.
source: These components capture the temporal modulations of the neural activity throughout the trial, irrespective of the task condition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what condition-independent components represent.

claim: Most encoding axes corresponding to different task parameters are close to orthogonal to each other.
source: Second, even though dPCA, unlike PCA, does not enforce orthogonality between encoding axes corresponding to different task parameters, most of them turned out to be close to orthogonal to each other (Figures 3–6e, upper triangle), as has been observed before (Brendel et al., 2011; Rishel et al., 2013; Raposo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3-6e and consistent with prior observations.

claim: All dPCA components in each dataset are distributed across the whole neural population.
source: Third, all dPCA components in each of the datasets are distributed across the whole neural population (as opposed to being exhibited only by a subset of cells).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7a.

claim: For each component, the distribution of encoder weights is strongly unimodal and centered at zero.
source: For each component, the distribution of weights is strongly unimodal, centred at zero (Figure 7a), and rather symmetric (although it is skewed to one side for some components).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7a.

claim: There are no distinct sub-populations of neurons predominantly expressing a particular component.
source: In other words, there are no distinct sub-populations of neurons predominantly expressing a particular component; rather, each individual neuron can be visualized as a random linear combination of these components.
evidence: This is inferred from the unimodal distributions in Figure 7a and clustering analysis in Figure 7b.

claim: Clustering analysis found only one cluster in all datasets.
source: We confirmed this observation by applying a recently developed clustering algorithm (Rodriguez and Laio, 2014) to the population of neurons in the 15-dimensional space of dPC weights. In all cases, the algorithm found only one cluster (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7b using a cited clustering method.

claim: The absence of detectable clusters of neurons has been noted before.
source: This absence of any detectable clusters of neurons has been noted before (Machens et al., 2010) and was recently observed in other datasets as well (Raposo et al., 2014).
evidence: This observation is consistent with prior work cited.

claim: dPCA combines the strengths of existing supervised and unsupervised approaches to neural population data analysis.
source: Demixed PCA combines the strengths of existing supervised and unsupervised approaches to neural population data analysis (Table 1, see also the first section of the Results).
evidence: This is a summary claim about the method's advantages, supported by Table 1 and the Results section.

claim: Supervised methods can characterize population tuning but often do not faithfully represent the whole dataset.
source: Supervised methods can characterize population tuning to various parameters of interest but often do not faithfully represent the whole dataset.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1 where supervised methods explain only 22-23% of variance.

claim: Unsupervised methods can capture overall variance but are not informed by task parameters.
source: Unsupervised methods can capture the overall variance but are not informed by task parameters.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1 where PCA captures more variance but shows mixed selectivity.

claim: dPCA yields components that capture almost as much variance as PCA but are demixed.
source: Our method yields components that capture almost as much variance as PCA does, but are demixed.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3-6c,d across all datasets.

claim: Demixing can greatly simplify visualization and interpretation of neural population data.
source: On one hand, demixing can greatly simplify visualization and interpretation of neural population data. Indeed, in all cases presented here, all the major aspects of the population activity that had previously been reported are directly visible on the dPCA summary figure.
evidence: This is demonstrated across Figures 3-6 where major findings from prior studies are reproduced.

claim: All major aspects of population activity that had previously been reported are directly visible on dPCA summary figures.
source: On one hand, demixing can greatly simplify visualization and interpretation of neural population data. Indeed, in all cases presented here, all the major aspects of the population activity that had previously been reported are directly visible on the dPCA summary figure.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 3-6 with citations to prior work.

claim: Faithful representation of population activity avoids interpretation bias that could be inherited by theoretical models.
source: On the other hand, faithful representation of the population activity (i.e. 'capturing variance') avoids that a particular interpretation distorts characteristic features of the data. The latter feature is particularly important for the development of theoretical models, which otherwise may inherit an interpretation bias without being aware of it.
evidence: This is a reasoning-based claim about the importance of capturing variance.

claim: dPCA highlights common features of neural activity when applied to several datasets.
source: Apart from being a useful tool for analyzing any particular dataset, dPCA highlights common features of neural activity when applied to several datasets, allowing to adopt a comparative approach to study population activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the comparative analysis across four datasets.

claim: The method presented here is conceptually based on previous work but is technically very different.
source: The method presented here is conceptually based on our previous work (Machens, 2010; Machens et al., 2010; Brendel et al., 2011), but is technically very different.
evidence: This is a statement comparing the current method with prior versions.

claim: The original approach from Machens et al. (2010) only works for two parameters of interest.
source: The original approach from Machens et al. (2010) only works for two parameters of interest, such as time and stimulus.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of prior work with citation.

claim: Removing the orthogonality constraint allowed obtaining a simple analytical solution in terms of singular value decompositions.
source: Third, removing the orthogonality constraint allowed us to obtain a simple analytical solution in terms of singular value decompositions (see Materials and methods) and hence to avoid local minima, convergence issues, and any additional optimization-related hyperparameters.
evidence: This is a technical claim about the mathematical properties of the new method.

claim: The current dPCA-2015 method achieves significantly higher demixing indices than dPCA-2011.
source: For all datasets, these indices were significantly higher with our current dPCA-2015 method than with dPCA-2011.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison shown in Figure 14.

claim: dPCA-2011 failed to find some weak components.
source: Moreover, dPCA-2011 failed to find some weak components at all.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 14.

claim: dPCA demixes task-parameter dependencies better than TDR.
source: Comparison of dPCA with TDR on our datasets shows that dPCA demixes the task-parameter dependencies better than TDR (see Figure 14 in the Materials and methods).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 14.

claim: dPCA as presented works only with discrete parameters.
source: First, dPCA as presented here works only with discrete parameters, and all possible parameter combinations must be present in the data.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the method.

claim: A dataset may be non-demixable if high-variance directions of stimulus and decision parts fully overlap.
source: Third, even with a large number of neurons, a dataset may be non-demixable, in which case dPCA would fail. For instance, if the high-variance directions of the stimulus and the decision parts of the neural activities fully overlap, then there is no linear decoder that can demix the two parameters.
evidence: This is a theoretical limitation based on the mathematical properties of the method.

claim: Successive dPCA components corresponding to the same parameter can be difficult to interpret due to orthogonality constraint.
source: Finally, dPCA components corresponding to the same parameter (e.g. successive stimulus components) are here chosen to be orthogonal, similarly to PCA. This can make successive components difficult to interpret (e.g. the second and the third stimulus components in Figure 3).
evidence: This is noted as a limitation with reference to Figure 3.

claim: All four datasets used in the manuscript have been made available at http://crcns.org.
source: All four datasets used in this manuscript have been made available at http://crcns.org (Romo et al., 2016; Constantinidis et al., 2016; Feierstein et al., 2016; Uchida et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a factual statement about data availability with citations.
